hints: Look at the functional groups on each pair. Ask yourself which pairs contain a C=C double bond and which contain two different reactive groups like OH with CO2H or COCl.
walkthrough:
Sort by what reacts**
Think of it like this. If the monomers have a C=C double bond, they can just add together with no small molecule lost. If they have pairs of functional groups such as alcohol plus carboxylic acid, or acyl chloride plus phenol, they join by losing a small molecule such as water or HCl.

Apply to the three rows**
$\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ plus $\text{HO}_2\text{CCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ is diol plus diacid, so polyester formation with loss of water, condensation. Terephthaloyl dichloride plus $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$ is diacyl chloride plus diol, again polyester with loss of HCl, condensation. $\text{CH}_3\text{CHCF}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CHCH}_2$ are both alkenes, they contain C=C, so they join by addition with no small molecule lost.

Final answer: Row 1: condensation
Row 2: condensation
Row 3: addition

hints: Recall what happens when the NH2 group of one amino acid meets the CO2H group of the next, and what small molecule is eliminated.
Think about how to line up three molecules of CH3CH(NH2)CO2H so that each NH links to the next C=O, keeping the CH3 side chain on every alpha carbon.
Remember how Cambridge wants a polymer section drawn, with free bonds at the ends and a clear bracket or label to show the smallest repeating piece.
walkthrough:
See the monomer as bifunctional**
2-aminopropanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2\text{)CO}_2\text{H}$, has both an amine and a carboxylic acid in the same molecule. That means one molecule can act as both partners. The $\text{-NH}_2$ of one attacks the $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ of the next, water is lost, and you get an amide link, $\text{-CONH-}$, also called a peptide link.

Build three in a row**
Line up three monomers head to tail: N to C to N to C. After losing two molecules of water you get $\text{---NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO---}$. Check every alpha carbon still carries $\text{CH}_3$ and H, and every link is $\text{NH-CO}$ correctly oriented. No other monomer is involved, so only Ala residues appear.

Finish the polymer convention**
Because this is a section of a longer chain, show continuation bonds sticking out at the left N end and the right C=O end. Then bracket or label one $\text{-NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-}$ unit as the repeat unit. That one unit is what repeats over and over to make the whole chain.

Final answer: Polypeptide: $\text{---NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO---}$ with correct amide links, three Ala residues only, continuation bonds at both ends and one repeat unit $\text{---NH-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO---}$ clearly identified.

hints: Focus on the central carbon of CH3CH(NH2)CO2H and count how many different groups are attached to it.
Recall the name given to stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images and need wedge and hashed bonds to show 3D shape.
walkthrough:
Spot why it must be chiral**
Draw the alpha carbon. It is bonded to four completely different groups: $\text{-NH}_2$, $\text{-CH}_3$, $\text{-H}$ and $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. Any carbon with four different groups is a chiral centre, so two non-superimposable mirror images exist.

Draw the mirror pair in 3D**
Keep the drawing tetrahedral, not flat. Put two bonds in the plane, one solid wedge coming out toward you and one hashed wedge going back. For the second isomer, simply swap the wedge and dash positions, for example $\text{NH}_2$ on a wedge in one and on a dash in the other, keeping all four groups the same. Label the type as optical isomerism, the enantiomeric pair.

Final answer: Two 3D tetrahedral structures with central C bonded to $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{H}$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, one with solid wedge and one with hashed wedge interchanged to give mirror images.
Type of stereoisomerism: optical isomerism.

hints: Look at the skeletal formula of W with its two three-membered epoxide rings and recall which two-part glue uses a diepoxide plus a hardener.
walkthrough:
Recognise the diepoxide clue**
Compound W has two epoxide rings, those strained three-membered rings with O. When a diepoxide is mixed with a hardener it crosslinks into a tough thermoset without any solvent evaporating. That classic two-part non-solvent adhesive is called an epoxy resin.

hints: Think of the simplest alkyl chain that can carry an NH2 group at each end so the two nitrogens are on different carbons and both can open epoxide rings.
walkthrough:
Design a linker with two ends**
The hardener must bridge between epoxide chains, so it needs two reactive amine groups in one molecule, but not on the same carbon. The simplest choice is 1,2-diaminoethane, $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Each $\text{-NH}_2$ can attack and open an epoxide ring, building the crosslinked network.
Final answer: $\text{H}_2\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ (any diamine with two $\text{-NH}_2$ groups on different carbons, e.g. $\text{H}_2\text{N(CH}_2\text{)}_n\text{NH}_2$).
